cards.front: Sequence of stages in new drug development
cards.text: Synthesis/isolation, then {{preclinical}} studies, then permission for {{clinical}} trials, formulation and standardisation, then phase I-III trials, then {{marketing}} permission, then phase {{IV}} surveillance.

cards.front: Short note: Orphan drugs

points: Drugs or biologicals for diagnosis, treatment or prevention of a rare disease, or of a common disease endemic only in resource-poor areas
No reasonable expectation that development costs will be recovered from sales
Life-saving for some patients but commercially hard to bring to market
Governments give incentives (USA Orphan Drug Act 1983: rare = fewer than 0.2 million people)

cards.front: What are the main ways a new drug is discovered?
cards.back: Natural sources (plants: opium, cinchona, ephedra; animals: insulin, thyroxine; microbes: penicillin), random chemical synthesis (rarely used now because the chance of hitting the wanted activity is very low), modification of a known lead compound, and rational target-based design aided by molecular modelling, combinatorial chemistry and biotechnology (recombinant DNA drugs). The trend is from chance finds toward designing against a known target.

cards.front: What is a lead compound and what is lead optimisation? Give examples.
cards.back: A lead is a compound with some wanted activity but imperfect properties. Lead optimisation makes congeners to raise potency or selectivity and cut toxicity, guided by structure-activity relationships. Examples: acetazolamide led to thiazide diuretics; phenothiazines to tricyclic antidepressants; histamine (side chain changed) to H2 blockers; isoprenaline to selective beta-2 agonists and beta blockers.

cards.front: Short note: Preclinical safety testing of a new drug

points: Primary activity in vitro and in animal models
Systemic pharmacology and mechanism of action
Animal pharmacokinetics
Acute: single escalating doses, animals observed 1-3 days; LD50 calculated; histopathology
Subacute: repeated doses for 2-12 weeks (by intended human duration)
Chronic: 6-12 months, usually alongside early clinical trials
Reproduction and teratogenicity: spermatogenesis, ovulation, fertility, foetus
Mutagenicity: Ames test, mammalian cell cultures and intact rodents
Carcinogenicity: long-term (lifetime) dosing in animals
At least two species (one rodent, one non-rodent), oral and parenteral routes
Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) standards

cards.front: Short note: Drug repositioning (repurposing)

points: Finding a new indication for an existing drug
Also called repurposing
Phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) starts from a genetic variant and asks which phenotypes it links to
Associations with variants in drug-target genes suggest new indications for existing drugs
The same approach can predict adverse effects of available or new drugs
Phase IV postmarketing studies give information on new indications, risks, and optimal doses and schedules

cards.front: Why are single-enantiomer drugs developed in place of racemates?
cards.back: The two enantiomers of a chiral drug can differ in activity: the inactive one may add side effects, toxicity or metabolic load, or even oppose the active one (dextro-dopa is more toxic than levodopa). Regulators therefore test enantiomers separately and withhold approval of a racemate unless the pure enantiomer is no better. Examples: esomeprazole, escitalopram, levofloxacin, S-amlodipine, cisatracurium.

cards.front: Why must animal toxicity be studied in two species, and which special toxicity tests follow the systemic tests?
cards.back: Species differ in drug handling and sensitivity (rabbits resist atropine, rats and mice resist digitalis), so at least one rodent and one non-rodent are used before results are extrapolated to humans. Systemic tests run acute, subacute and chronic. Special tests then check reproduction and teratogenicity, mutagenicity (Ames test, cell cultures) and carcinogenicity (long-term dosing). Studies follow Good Laboratory Practice.

cards.front: Essay: Stages of new drug development from discovery to post-marketing

points: Complex, costly, risky: at least 10 years and 500-1000 million US dollars per drug
Most candidates fail along the way
Natural sources: opium, ephedra, cinchona, curare, belladonna, qinghaosu
Modification of known drugs; lead optimisation
Rational target-based design, molecular modelling, biotechnology
Screening, systemic pharmacology, animal pharmacokinetics
Acute, subacute and chronic toxicity
Reproductive, mutagenic and carcinogenic testing under GLP
Investigational new drug (IND) permission from the regulatory authority
Ethics committee approval; GCP (ICH); national ethical guidelines (ICMR in India); Declaration of Helsinki
Phase 0 (optional microdosing)
Phase I: safety and pharmacokinetics
Phase II: efficacy and dose range
Phase III: confirmatory comparative trials, then NDA
Review and marketing permission (0.5-2 years); restricted permission for toxic but useful drugs
Phase IV post-marketing surveillance; new indications, dosage forms and combinations

cards.front: Compare serendipity, lead modification and rational design as routes to a new drug, with an example of each.
cards.back: Serendipity: activity found by chance in random synthesis or screening (barbiturates, chlorpromazine); a poor hit rate, so little used now. Lead modification: improve a known molecule (acetazolamide to thiazides, histamine to H2 blockers); predictable, gives me-better drugs. Rational design: start from a known target or disease mechanism (COX-2 structure gave selective COX-2 inhibitors; reverse transcriptase gave anti-HIV drugs; striatal dopamine deficiency gave levodopa); can open a truly new class, but needs the target identified first. Every route then passes through the same preclinical and clinical gates.

cards.front: The four grades of strength of clinical evidence
cards.text: Grade I = {{systematic reviews / meta-analyses}}; Grade II = {{well-powered randomised controlled trials}}; Grade III = {{open-label, pilot and observational (cohort, case-control) studies}}; Grade IV = {{case reports and anecdotal experience}}.

cards.front: The phases of clinical trials
cards.text: Phase {{I}} = first human study, safety and pharmacokinetics; Phase {{II}} = therapeutic exploration and dose ranging; Phase {{III}} = randomised confirmatory comparison; Phase {{IV}} = post-marketing surveillance.

cards.front: Clinical study designs in drug research
cards.text: The three types of clinical study are {{clinical trial}}, {{cohort study}} and {{case-control study}}. A cohort study compares outcomes in users and {{non-users}} of a drug.

cards.front: What is a phase 0 (microdosing) study?
cards.back: An optional exploratory study before phase I. A sub-pharmacological microdose (about 1/100 of the expected therapeutic dose, at most 100 micrograms) is given to a few healthy volunteers, and ultra-low drug levels are measured by accelerator mass spectrometry or LC-MS/MS. Purpose: early human pharmacokinetics to drop poor candidates cheaply. Limitation: kinetics at microdoses may not match therapeutic doses; it gives no efficacy or safety data.

cards.front: What is a clinical trial, and what must be in place before it begins?
cards.back: A prospective, ethical study in humans that compares groups treated in different ways to answer a precise question. Before it starts: approval by an independent ethics committee under Good Clinical Practice (ICH) and national (ICMR) guidelines, consistent with the Declaration of Helsinki, and written informed consent from every participant. The committee checks autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice.

cards.front: Why is randomised, double-blind design the strongest clinical trial method?
cards.back: Randomisation removes investigator or patient selection bias and balances known and unknown confounders. Double blinding keeps both patient and investigator unaware of allocation, limiting conscious and unconscious bias in outcome assessment. Together they give the most credible evidence of efficacy and safety.

cards.front: Which study design is used to detect a suspected rare adverse drug event, and what is its main weakness?
cards.back: A case-control study: patients with the event are compared with matched controls for past drug exposure. It is quick and cheap for rare events, but it cannot prove causation, depends on retrospective records and is prone to bias. Cohort studies, by contrast, can reveal unsuspected events.

cards.front: Short note: Phases of clinical drug trials

points: About 1/100 of the estimated human dose (max 100 micrograms) in healthy volunteers
Early human pharmacokinetics only; not established or mandatory

sections.h: Phase I: human pharmacology and safety
points: First human use; 20-80 subjects, mostly healthy volunteers (sometimes patients); open label
Start at 1/100 to 1/10 of the highest non-toxic animal dose and increase stepwise
Aims: safety, tolerability, human pharmacokinetics, dose range

sections.h: Phase II: therapeutic exploration and dose ranging
points: 100-500 patients at 2-4 centres; mostly controlled and randomised
Establishes efficacy, dose range and ceiling effect
Many candidates are dropped here
500-3000 patients; randomised double-blind comparative, multicentre
Value relative to existing therapy; indications finalised
New drug application (NDA) to the licensing authority for marketing permission
Data from practising doctors in real-world use
Detects rare, long-term and interaction adverse effects
Studies in special groups; new indications, dosage forms and combinations

cards.front: Short note: Off-label use of drugs

points: Prescribing a drug for a use outside the package-insert indication
The physician is not bound by the package insert
In the US a physician may legally prescribe a drug for any purpose judged reasonable
Third-party payers generally do not reimburse off-label use unless a named compendium supports the new use
Physician may face litigation if harm follows an unapproved use
Company promotion must stay within the package insert
Rofecoxib was approved for acute pain for up to 5 days but was widely prescribed off-label for chronic pain
The high dose (50 mg/day) was linked to a 5-fold increase in myocardial infarction risk

cards.front: What do randomisation and blinding each control, and how are the common trial designs compared?
cards.back: Randomisation (including stratified randomisation by age, sex or severity) balances known and unknown confounders and prevents selection bias. Blinding hides allocation: single-blind keeps the subject unaware, double-blind keeps subject and investigator unaware, with the code held by a third party. Designs: parallel group (test and control run together) versus crossover (each subject is own control, smaller sample, but carry-over effect and only suited to stable chronic disease); sequential and multicentric designs speed results; non-inferiority trials show the new drug is not worse.

cards.front: How are type I error, type II error, power and sample size related in a trial?
cards.back: Type I error is finding a difference that does not exist (its probability is the significance level, e.g. 0.05). Type II error is missing a real difference; power is its complement, so power 0.9 means a 10% chance of missing it. Sample size is calculated from significance level, power, the clinically significant difference and the variability of the end point; a smaller expected difference or greater variation needs more subjects.

cards.front: Essay: Clinical trial design and control of bias

points: Answer precisely framed questions by comparing equivalent groups treated by two or more modalities
Healthy volunteers for PK and tolerability; patients for most efficacy questions
Approval by an independent ethics committee; Good Clinical Practice (ICH) guidelines
National ethical guidelines (ICMR in India); Declaration of Helsinki
Written informed consent
Principles: autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice
Control group: placebo (if ethical) or standard treatment (active control)
Parallel group vs cross-over (subjects as own controls; carry-over effects; only for stable chronic diseases)
Inclusion/exclusion criteria, dose regimen and sample size fixed in advance
Superiority or non-inferiority aims
Randomisation (simple or stratified by age, sex, severity)
Blinding: single or double; allocation code held by a third party
Pre-specified end points and statistical plan
Type I (alpha) error: false difference; type II (beta) error: missed real difference
Results apply only to the population and dose regimen studied; dose-ranging needs separate trials

cards.front: A new drug passes phase III but a rare serious adverse effect appears after marketing. Why was it missed and how is it found?
cards.back: Phase III enrols only 500-3000 selected patients for limited periods, so very rare reactions, delayed effects and effects in children, elderly or pregnant patients stay invisible. Phase IV postmarketing surveillance in large unselected populations detects them. A cohort study (users versus non-users) can reveal unsuspected adverse events; a case-control study tests a suspected link by comparing affected patients with matched controls for past exposure.

cards.front: How should the dose of a renally excreted drug be altered in renal impairment?
cards.back: Loading dose is generally kept unchanged (unless oedema is present). The maintenance dose is reduced in proportion to creatinine clearance, or the dosing interval is lengthened. Examples: aminoglycosides, digoxin, phenobarbitone. Drugs partly excreted unchanged need smaller reductions.

cards.front: Why must a dose always be stated with the response it is meant to produce?
cards.back: A drug has different effective doses for different effects, and prophylactic, therapeutic and toxic doses of the same drug differ. Example: aspirin 0.3-0.6 g for headache, 60-150 mg/day for antiplatelet action, 3-5 g/day for rheumatoid arthritis. Recommended doses come from population data for an average patient, so individual patients need adjustment.

cards.front: What is cumulation and which drugs are particularly prone to it?
cards.back: Any drug accumulates when the rate of administration exceeds the rate of elimination; slowly eliminated drugs are most liable and cause cumulative toxicity (chloroquine retinal damage on prolonged use). Practical rules: do not give a full digoxin loading dose if one was taken in the past week, and do not repeat an emetine course within 6 weeks.

cards.front: What is rational prescribing and what are its criteria?
cards.back: WHO: patients get medicines suited to their clinical need, in individual doses, for adequate time, at lowest cost to them and the community. Criteria: appropriate indication, appropriate drug (efficacy, safety, suitability, cost), appropriate dose, route and duration, an appropriate patient, correct dispensing with information, and monitoring of adherence, benefit and adverse effects. Knowing the drug alone does not make prescribing rational.

cards.front: What are the strategies for individualising drug dose, and which fits which drug?
cards.back: Four strategies. 1) Standard dose: one dose suits nearly everyone because variation is small or the safety margin is wide (penicillin, oral contraceptives, chloroquine). 2) Regulated dose: the drug modifies an easily measured body function, so dose is adjusted to that reading (antihypertensives, hypoglycaemics, anticoagulants, diuretics); plasma levels are not needed. 3) Target-level dose: response is hard to measure but tied to a plasma range, so an empirical dose is later adjusted by drug-level monitoring (digoxin, antiepileptics, antidepressants, theophylline). 4) Titrated dose: the full effect cannot be given because of adverse effects, so dose is titrated to a tolerable level of toxicity (anticancer drugs, corticosteroids, levodopa).

cards.front: Short note: Fixed dose combinations (FDCs)

points: Two or more drugs given in a fixed ratio in one preparation
Convenience and better adherence; can be cheaper
Synergy: sulfamethoxazole with trimethoprim, levodopa with carbidopa, isoniazid with rifampin
Components with different mechanisms (amlodipine with atenolol) add effect without adding the same side effects
Avoids giving one drug alone in TB, HIV and falciparum malaria
Patient may not need every component; dose of each cannot be adjusted separately
Components may have different time courses and be differently affected by kidney or liver disease
Hard to tell which drug caused an adverse effect; allergy to one component bars the whole product
Fosters false confidence, especially with antimicrobial combinations; corticosteroids should never be combined with other internal-use drugs
Only a handful of FDCs are rational
Each ingredient must be needed; never justified to give an unneeded drug to supply another
Many irrational FDCs have been banned in India

cards.front: Short note: Chronopharmacology (time of dosing)

points: Drug response depends on the time of administration, which is linked to the body's circadian rhythm
Circadian control extends to hormone release (GH, prolactin, ACTH)
Statins inhibit cholesterol synthesis more when taken in the late evening
A single morning corticosteroid dose causes less pituitary-adrenal suppression
Hypnotics work more easily when taken at night
Quick-release bromocriptine, taken early in the morning, is used in type 2 diabetes
Pineal hormone secreted at night that synchronises the sleep-wake cycle
Used mainly for jet lag and shift work; not a dependable hypnotic

cards.front: How do you choose between titrated and target-level dosing for a drug?
cards.back: Ask what can be measured. If response is hard to measure but a plasma range is known to work (digoxin, antiepileptics, theophylline), aim at the target level and adjust by monitoring. If the maximal effect cannot be given because of toxicity (anticancer drugs, corticosteroids, levodopa), titrate to a tolerable level of adverse effect: low start and upward titration in non-critical illness, high start and downward titration in critical illness.

cards.front: Short note: Process of rational prescribing and common irrationalities

points: Diagnose (at least provisionally); define the therapeutic problem and goal
Choose the drug class, then the drug by efficacy, safety, suitability and cost
Decide route, dose and duration; give information and instructions
Monitor adherence, goal attainment and adverse events; modify therapy
Drug used when none is needed (antibiotics for viral fever)
Wrong drug, wrong route (injection when oral works), wrong dose or duration
Needless combinations, expensive newer drugs, polypharmacy ignoring interactions
Delayed cure, more adverse effects, microbial resistance, cost, loss of trust

cards.front: Short note: How organ disease changes drug dosing

points: First-pass bioavailability rises; albumin falls so more free acidic drug
Metabolism of morphine, lidocaine, propranolol falls: reduce dose
Prefer oxazepam, lorazepam, atenolol; prodrugs needing activation work poorly
Reduce maintenance dose or lengthen interval with creatinine clearance; loading dose usually unchanged
Examples: aminoglycosides, digoxin, phenobarbitone
Avoid pethidine, nephrotoxic drugs; thiazides fail, use furosemide
Absorption falls, elimination slows; lower loading doses of lidocaine, procainamide; digitalis sensitivity rises
Hypothyroid: more sensitive to digoxin and morphine; hyperthyroid: resistant to digoxin inotropy

cards.front: Essay: Factors that modify drug response and how to individualise therapy

points: Variation between patients and within the same patient
Changes can be quantitative (concentration/effect) or qualitative (allergy, idiosyncrasy)
Body size, age, sex and pregnancy
Genetics (pharmacogenetics)
Disease states: renal, hepatic, cardiac, thyroid
Tolerance, cumulation and drug interactions
Route of administration and formulation
Timing relative to meals and circadian factors
Placebo and nocebo responses
Enzyme inducers from diet or smoking
Choose drug and dose according to the factors above
Start with a standard or target-level dose, then adjust by response or drug levels
Monitor and document response in the individual

cards.front: Why is body weight or body surface area used for dosing in children and very obese or lean adults?
cards.back: Adult doses assume a medium build. Paediatric and atypical-build doses are scaled to body weight (weight / 70 x adult dose). BSA is physiologically closer to water and metabolic mass but has limited dosing data, so weight is the usual index (BSA is used mainly for anticancer drugs). Dubois: BSA = 0.007184 x W^0.425 x H^0.725.

cards.front: Why do newborns clear renally excreted drugs slowly?
cards.back: Newborn GFR is low and tubular transport immature, so half-life of drugs excreted by filtration (gentamicin) or secretion (penicillin) is prolonged 3-5 times. GFR reaches adult rates by about 5 months and tubular secretion matures by about 7 months. Hepatic metabolism is also inadequate, and the blood-brain barrier is more permeable (kernicterus). Infant doses must be learned, not derived by formula.

cards.front: Why must doses of renally cleared drugs be cut in the elderly?
cards.back: Nephron loss lowers GFR to about 75% of the young-adult value at 50 years and about 50% at 75 years, so such drugs accumulate. Example: streptomycin 0.75 g daily after 50 years and 0.5 g after 70, against 1 g in young adults. Reduced liver metabolism and blood flow add to cumulative toxicity on prolonged use.

cards.front: Which adverse effects are special to children?
cards.back: Growing tissue is vulnerable: corticosteroids suppress growth; androgens cause early epiphyseal fusion and stunting; tetracyclines deposit in growing teeth, discolouring and deforming them; phenothiazines cause dystonic reactions more often. Solid dosage forms and metered inhalers are hard for young children, while rectal diazepam solution (fast, predictable absorption) controls febrile seizures under 5 years.

cards.front: Why is chloramphenicol dangerous in neonates (grey baby syndrome)?
cards.back: Neonatal hepatic conjugation (glucuronidation) is immature, so the drug accumulates. Result: abdominal distension, vasomotor collapse, cyanosis and grey skin. Also, the newborn has low GFR and immature tubular function, which prolongs half-life of renally cleared drugs.

cards.front: Short note: Dose adjustment in children and the elderly

points: Dose by body weight; infant absorption and skin permeability differ
Immature renal function prolongs elimination of renally cleared drugs
Grey baby syndrome with chloramphenicol
Faster metabolism after infancy: shorter half-life, higher mg/kg dose
Falling GFR with age; reduce renally cleared drugs
Reduced hepatic metabolism and liver blood flow; risk of cumulative toxicity
Lower albumin: changed protein binding
Higher sensitivity to CNS and anticholinergic effects; more drug interactions (polypharmacy)

cards.front: How does pregnancy change drug disposition?
cards.back: Reduced GI motility delays absorption; plasma and extracellular fluid expand, raising volume of distribution; albumin falls while alpha-1 acid glycoprotein rises, so unbound acidic drugs rise and basic ones fall; renal blood flow rises, speeding polar drug removal; hepatic enzyme induction speeds metabolism. The net effect is complex and hard to predict.

cards.front: Why are adverse reactions commoner in the elderly, and how do you prescribe safely for them?
cards.back: Cause chain: lower GFR and hepatic clearance cause accumulation; lower albumin raises free drug; volume of distribution shifts (up for lipophilic, down for hydrophilic drugs); receptor responsiveness changes (digitalis poorly tolerated, adrenergic responses reduced); prostatism makes even mild anticholinergic action cause retention; polypharmacy multiplies interactions and brings postural instability, giddiness and confusion. Safe practice: reduce renally cleared doses, review the drug list and monitor.

cards.front: What is the pharmacogenetic risk with TPMT deficiency?
cards.back: Low thiopurine methyltransferase activity raises the risk of severe bone marrow toxicity with 6-mercaptopurine and azathioprine. Poor-metaboliser status for NUDT15 has the same effect; TPMT poor metabolisers are rare in East Asians, who instead more often carry NUDT15 variants.

cards.front: Pharmacogenetic examples (drug, gene or enzyme, consequence)
cards.text: G6PD deficiency: {{primaquine}} haemolysis; TPMT deficiency: {{azathioprine}} marrow toxicity; CYP2D6 poor metaboliser: {{codeine}} fails to give analgesia; CYP2C9 variant: {{warfarin}} bleeding; NAT2 slow acetylator: {{isoniazid}} neuropathy.

cards.front: Define pharmacogenetics, pharmacogenomics and SNP.
cards.back: Pharmacogenetics: study of the genetic basis of variable drug response and handling. Pharmacogenomics: use of genetic information to choose drug and dose for an individual (personalised medicine). SNP: single base-pair substitution found in more than 1% of a population. Most drugs show bell-shaped (Gaussian) variation, with specific genetic defects adding discontinuous variation.

cards.front: What is the clinical effect of slow acetylator status (NAT2)?
cards.back: NAT2 polymorphism creates rapid and slow acetylators. Slow acetylators accumulate drugs cleared by acetylation, so isoniazid neuropathy and procainamide- or hydralazine-induced lupus occur mainly in them.

cards.front: Which drugs are classically linked to haemolysis in G6PD deficiency, and how is the trait inherited?
cards.back: X-linked monogenic trait, commoner in Mediterranean, African and Southeast Asian people. Oxidising drugs trigger haemolysis, e.g. primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamides/cotrimoxazole, nitrofurantoin, chloramphenicol, quinine, methylene blue. Haemolysis is largely dose-related, and its severity varies with the gene variant (worst in homozygous deficient individuals).

cards.front: Why does codeine fail to relieve pain in some patients? (CYP2D6)
cards.back: Codeine is a prodrug: CYP2D6 converts it to morphine, which gives the analgesia. Poor CYP2D6 metabolisers form little morphine, so analgesia is absent. Ultrarapid metabolisers form excess morphine and may develop features of opioid excess, including respiratory depression.

cards.front: Short note: Pharmacogenetics in drug therapy

points: Pharmacogenetics: genetic basis of variable drug response
Pharmacogenomics: use of genetic information to guide choice of drug and dose
Polymorphisms of drug-metabolising enzymes (CYP2D6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, NAT2, TPMT, pseudocholinesterase)
Variants of drug targets (VKORC1 for warfarin) and transporters (P-gp)
HLA alleles causing immune hypersensitivity; enzyme deficiencies such as G6PD
Succinylcholine apnoea: atypical pseudocholinesterase
Warfarin bleeding and lower dose need: CYP2C9 and VKORC1 variants
Clopidogrel (prodrug) ineffective in CYP2C19 poor metabolisers: use an alternative antiplatelet
Isoniazid neuropathy; hydralazine and procainamide lupus: slow acetylators
Carbamazepine and phenytoin with HLA-B*15:02 (East and South Asians); abacavir with HLA-B*57:01; allopurinol with HLA-B*58:01
Malignant hyperthermia after halothane: ryanodine receptor defect
Monogenic traits predict response well; polygenic traits poorly

cards.front: Which genetic variants predict chemotherapy toxicity or resistance?
cards.back: UGT1A1*28 allele (low glucuronyl transferase) raises irinotecan neutropenia and diarrhoea; DPD (dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase) deficiency causes severe 5-fluorouracil toxicity; TPMT deficiency causes marrow toxicity with 6-mercaptopurine and azathioprine; P-glycoprotein overexpression pumps drugs out of tumour cells and causes resistance.

cards.front: Genetic defects that make a drug dangerous
cards.text: Atypical pseudocholinesterase: prolonged {{succinylcholine}} apnoea; abnormal ryanodine receptor: {{halothane}} malignant hyperthermia; acute intermittent porphyria: precipitated by {{barbiturates}}; abnormal VKOR enzyme: resistance to {{coumarin}} anticoagulants; inability to hydroxylate: {{phenytoin}} toxicity at usual doses.

cards.front: Why is routine genotyping to guide drug therapy still limited, and where does it work best?
cards.back: Dose may vary 4-6 fold between people and all determinants of response (transporters, enzymes, channels, receptors) are genetically controlled, yet practice is limited because each drug needs its own genotype screen and much variability is unexplained. Genotype predicts phenotype best for monogenic traits (G6PD, CYP2D6, TPMT), poorly for polygenic ones. Genotyping is needed only once in life; simple spot tests (G6PD) are already used.

cards.front: One patient gets no pain relief from codeine and another develops marrow failure on azathioprine. Explain each.
cards.back: Codeine is a prodrug converted to morphine by CYP2D6; a poor metaboliser forms little morphine, so no analgesia. Azathioprine is cleared by TPMT; deficiency (and NUDT15 variants, which also alter thiopurine metabolite levels) leaves toxic thiopurine levels and marrow toxicity. In both the gene alters drug handling, not receptor action, so genotype-guided drug choice or dose reduction is the remedy.

cards.front: Define placebo and nocebo, and name one placebo use in a trial.
cards.back: Placebo: an inert substance given as if it were active; its effect comes from the therapeutic setting and expectation (psychodynamic). Nocebo: a negative response driven by pessimism or loss of faith in the drug or doctor. A placebo serves as the dummy control in a clinical trial.

cards.front: What is tachyphylaxis and which drugs show it most?
cards.back: Rapid loss of response when doses are repeated closely. It is seen most with indirect sympathomimetics (ephedrine, tyramine, nicotine), which work by releasing catecholamines; the stores are depleted faster than they are refilled.

cards.front: What is tolerance and what are its types?
cards.back: Need for a higher dose to get the same response. Natural: species or individual inherently less sensitive (rabbits to atropine). Acquired: develops with repeated use in an initially responsive person, most evident with CNS depressants. Refractoriness is loss of efficacy after prolonged use (sulfonylureas in type 2 diabetes, agonists in asthma). Little or none develops to atropine, digoxin, cocaine or nitroprusside.

cards.front: What is cross tolerance? Give examples.
cards.back: Tolerance to pharmacologically related drugs; the closer two drugs are, the more complete. Alcoholics tolerate barbiturates and general anaesthetics. Morphine and barbiturates show partial cross tolerance, but morphine and pethidine show complete cross tolerance.

cards.front: What is the difference between pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic tolerance?
cards.back: Pharmacokinetic tolerance: less drug reaches the site, usually because elimination is enhanced, e.g. enzyme induction by barbiturates and carbamazepine. Pharmacodynamic (cellular) tolerance: target cells become less responsive, e.g. morphine, barbiturates, nitrates; due to receptor desensitisation or down-regulation, or weaker response effectuation.

cards.front: Short note: Tolerance and refractoriness

points: Tolerance: a larger dose is needed to produce the same effect
Refractoriness: loss of efficacy after prolonged or intensive use (sulfonylureas in type 2 diabetes; beta-2 agonists in asthma)
Natural: inherent low sensitivity (rabbits to atropine; some people to alcohol)
Acquired: repeated use; obvious with CNS depressants; little or none with atropine, digoxin, cocaine, nitroprusside
Cross tolerance between related drugs (alcoholics to barbiturates and general anaesthetics)
Tachyphylaxis: rapid tolerance on closely repeated doses (ephedrine, tyramine, nicotine)
Pharmacokinetic: enzyme induction, faster elimination
Pharmacodynamic: receptor desensitisation or down-regulation, weaker response effectuation, homeostatic adaptation
Chlorpromazine: to sedation but not antipsychotic action
Phenobarbitone: to sedation more than antiepileptic action
Morphine: to analgesia and euphoria more than to constipation and miosis

cards.front: How does a placebo work, where is it used, and what limits it?
cards.back: It acts through psychodynamic, not pharmacodynamic, means: the whole therapeutic setting and physician-patient relation matter. It can release endorphins (placebo analgesia is blocked by naloxone). Uses: dummy control in trials, and rarely for a patient who needs no active drug. Common placebos are lactose tablets and distilled water injection. Responses vary even in one person (sleep on night one, not later), so practical value is limited; nocebo is the negative counterpart.

cards.front: Tolerance does not develop equally to all effects of a drug. What follows for therapy?
cards.back: The therapeutic index may rise or fall with prolonged use. Chlorpromazine: tolerance to sedation but not antipsychotic action (index improves). Phenobarbitone: tolerance to sedation, less to antiepileptic action. Morphine: tolerance to analgesia and euphoria, little to constipation and miosis (index worsens). So dose escalation can raise toxicity without matching benefit.

cards.front: Compare tolerance, tachyphylaxis, refractoriness and drug resistance.
cards.back: Tolerance: gradual need for higher dose, by pharmacokinetic (induced elimination, e.g. carbamazepine) or pharmacodynamic (receptor desensitisation or down-regulation) mechanisms. Tachyphylaxis: rapid tolerance on closely repeated doses, typical of indirect sympathomimetics (ephedrine, tyramine, nicotine) whose catecholamine stores deplete. Refractoriness: loss of efficacy after prolonged intensive use. Drug resistance: tolerance of microorganisms to antimicrobials (staphylococci to penicillin).

cards.front: Essay: Comprehensive plan for drug development to meet an unmet need: diabetes mellitus

points: Type 2 diabetes is over 90% of cases; insulin resistance plus beta-cell failure
Existing agents: insulin needs multiple daily injections, hypoglycaemia and weight gain
Many patients cannot reach normoglycaemia; concern about hyperinsulinaemia and premature atherosclerosis
Rational approach: choose a target (insulin resistance, insulin secretion, incretin or glucose handling) and find a lead that binds it
Lead sources: natural products, lead optimisation of congeners, combinatorial chemistry with high-throughput screening (high failure rate), biotechnology (recombinant insulin, monoclonal antibodies)
Screening and pharmacodynamic tests; hypoglycaemic activity in animal models
Pharmacokinetics and acute, subacute and chronic toxicity in a rodent and a non-rodent
Reproductive toxicity, mutagenicity and carcinogenicity studies before human use
IND licence, then Phase I (safety, PK), Phase II (dose range, efficacy), Phase III (randomised, double-blind, comparative, larger population)
Surrogate endpoints such as HbA1c shorten trials; FDA expects cardiovascular safety data (rosiglitazone precedent)
Marketing permission follows Phase III, with indications finalised; drugs may be restricted to hospitals or specialists
Phase IV surveillance for rare and long-term adverse effects and interactions
Trials in special groups (children, elderly, renal impairment) and new formulations or combinations

cards.front: What are the main limitations of current drugs in type 2 diabetes?
cards.back: Insulin needs multiple daily injections and can cause hypoglycaemia and weight gain. Sulfonylureas, biguanides, thiazolidinediones and the others, apart from DPP-4 inhibitors and GLP-1 agonists, share these problems and often fail to achieve normoglycaemia alone. Insulin excess is also linked to premature atherosclerosis. These gaps define the unmet need.

cards.front: What is a surrogate endpoint and why is it used in premarketing trials?
cards.back: A biomarker or other measure believed to mediate or predict the true clinical endpoint (survival, disease prevention, symptoms, function). It shortens or shrinks trials. Examples: blood pressure, lipid levels, HbA1c and CD4 count. Some are excellent predictors (HIV RNA load), others have misled.

cards.front: Why did the FDA require larger cardiovascular safety data for new antidiabetic drugs?
cards.back: Rosiglitazone was approved in 1999 on short-term glycaemic trials. A 2007 meta-analysis of randomised trials then linked it to more myocardial infarctions. The FDA responded by asking that new antidiabetic trials exclude a cardiovascular risk increase of 30% or more; a two-stage route allowed premarketing trials to exclude 80% with postmarketing studies completing the 30% margin.

cards.front: Short note: Integrated approach in pharmacotherapy

points: Rational prescribing is a whole therapeutic set-up, not only choosing the right drug
Knowledge alone does not guarantee rational use: role models, patient load and drug promotion also shape prescribing
Diagnose (at least provisionally), define the problem and goal
Choose the class, then the drug on efficacy, safety, suitability and cost
Decide route, dose and duration; instruct the patient
Monitor adherence, goal attainment and adverse effects; modify therapy
Body size, age (neonatal and elderly clearance), sex, race, genetics
Pathological states: renal, hepatic, cardiac and thyroid disease alter disposition or sensitivity
Other drugs, cumulation and tolerance
Drug when none is needed; wrong drug, route, dose or duration
Needless combinations and polypharmacy without regard to interactions

cards.front: Which patient-related factors change the response to the same drug dose?
cards.back: Body size (weight or body surface area), age, sex, species and race, genetic make-up, route, environment and timing relative to meals, psychological expectation, disease states, other drugs, cumulation and tolerance. These act quantitatively (plasma level or effect changes, adjusted by dose) or qualitatively (allergy or idiosyncrasy).

cards.front: Short note: Biomarkers in clinical evaluation of drugs

points: A measurable indicator that anticipates a therapeutic or adverse response to a drug
Surrogates are biomarkers used as stand-ins for the real clinical outcome
Genetic markers: G-6PD deficiency (spot test), CYP2D6, TPMT and NAT2 polymorphisms
Disease or response markers: HbA1c, blood pressure, lipids, CD4 count, HIV RNA load
Monitoring markers that show progress or failure of treatment
Reduce the size and duration of premarketing trials
Expedited programmes such as Accelerated Approval can rest on surrogate endpoints
Some surrogates predict outcome well, others mislead
A drug can alter the marker without changing survival or symptoms
Genotype testing is limited by the need for drug-specific screening

cards.front: Define a biomarker and say how it differs from a surrogate endpoint.
cards.back: A biomarker is any measurable marker (genetic, biochemical or imaging) that predicts or tracks drug response, therapeutic or adverse. A surrogate endpoint is a biomarker chosen to replace the clinical endpoint in a trial, so it must reliably predict that endpoint.

cards.front: Why is G-6PD status a useful pre-treatment biomarker?
cards.back: G-6PD deficiency is an X-linked monogenic trait. Oxidant drugs such as primaquine, dapsone and sulfonamides cause haemolysis in deficient people, and the risk depends on the variant. A simple spot test identifies deficiency before the drug is given, which makes it a practical clinical biomarker.

cards.front: Short note: Features of an ideal randomised clinical trial

points: Precise, pre-specified objective with primary and secondary end points fixed in advance
Population set by inclusion and exclusion criteria; results apply only to that population
Control arm is the comparator against which the test drug is judged
Randomised allocation; stratify by age, sex or disease severity where needed
Single blind (subject unaware) or double blind (subject and investigator unaware)
Look-alike preparations; allocation code held by a third data-management party and opened after analysis
Fixed beforehand from significance level, power, the clinically meaningful difference and variability of the end point
Minimum number that still gives a decisive answer, for cost and ethical reasons
Independent committee can stop early on a decisive result or if one arm is clearly inferior

sections.h: Why it is the strongest design
points: Randomised double-blind controlled trial is the most credible source of evidence on efficacy, safety and comparative value

cards.front: Essay: Design and conduct of a 6-month repeated-dose toxicity study for a new drug

points: Characterise the toxicity profile on repeated dosing, identify target organs and the dose-response relation
Find the maximum recommended starting dose for the first human use
Clinical use beyond 3 months needs repeated-dose studies of 6 months in a rodent and in a non-rodent
Regulators may ask for 12 months or accept 6 months case by case
At least one rodent and one non-rodent, chosen on pharmacokinetic similarity to humans
Same route as the intended clinical use; run under Good Laboratory Practice
Highest dose: produces observable toxicity
Intermediate dose: some symptoms but no gross toxicity or death, placed logarithmically between the other two
Lowest dose: no observable toxicity
Cage-side observations, body weight, food and water intake
Blood biochemistry and haematology; renal parameters (urea, creatinine, urine specific gravity)
Non-rodents: electrocardiogram and fundus examination
Gross and microscopic examination of all viscera and tissues; injection sites if given parenterally
Reproduction and teratogenicity; mutagenicity battery (Ames test, in vitro chromosome or mouse lymphoma assay, mouse micronucleus)
Carcinogenicity studies are needed when expected clinical use is about 6 months or longer
Local tolerance at sites of contact

cards.front: Short note: Evaluating the hypersensitivity potential of a new drug

points: Allergic reactions are immune-mediated and not predicted by the drug's pharmacology
Single-dose tests miss them: prior sensitisation is needed and a latent period of 1-2 weeks follows the first exposure
Checks tolerance at every body site the drug touches
Separates mechanical or physicochemical irritation from true toxicological or pharmacodynamic effects
Local lymph node assay: compares lymphocyte proliferation in treated and control groups
Stimulation index of at least 3 is needed before a substance is judged a potential skin sensitiser
Patch tests confirm non-irritancy in people, and are used only after the chemical passes the in vitro non-corrosion and mutagenicity screens
Hypersensitivity findings feed the safety profile and the monitoring plan for trials and marketing

cards.front: What is the local lymph node assay and what result flags a skin sensitiser?
cards.back: An animal test for skin sensitisation that compares lymphocyte proliferation in treated and control groups after topical exposure. A stimulation index of at least 3 means the substance needs further evaluation as a potential skin sensitiser.

cards.front: What is a non-inferiority trial?
cards.back: A trial that tries to show the new drug is not clinically worse than an existing treatment. Superior efficacy is not required; the new drug may still be useful if it offers better tolerability, safety, convenience, cost or use in a special subgroup.

cards.front: What is a biomarker?
cards.back: A measurable characteristic that indicates a normal biological process, a disease process, or the response to an exposure or treatment. It can be molecular, histologic, radiographic or physiologic.
refs: WEB NeuroRx Biomarkers: Potential Uses and Limitations 2004 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC534923/

cards.front: Short note: Ideal biomarker, types and uses

points: Reliable and repeatable across tests and laboratories
Valid: reflects the biological process and the disease
Good sensitivity and specificity
Precise and objective, less biased than questionnaires
Stable during storage and transport
Affordable, feasible to collect, low risk to participants
Disease-associated: susceptibility/risk, diagnostic, prognostic, monitoring
Drug-related: predictive, pharmacodynamic/response, safety
Diagnosis and screening, including early disease
Prognosis: likelihood of developing or progressing
Monitoring severity and response to treatment
Trials: reduce heterogeneity and act as trial endpoints
Safety: e.g. liver enzymes for hepatotoxicity monitoring
